articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a cloud networking solutions provider headquartered in North Carolina. The settlement addresses nine instances between September 2018 and March 2022 where Extreme exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard, a Russian defense manufacturer.

JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard is blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated entity JSC Concern Almaz Antey. OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed by Extreme Networks but were also egregious.

This enforcement action highlights the critical importance for U.S. exporters and technology firms to conduct thorough end-user screening and beneficial ownership checks to ensure compliance with sanctions against Russian entities. The settlement amount reflects the egregious nature of the violations despite the company's self-reporting.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing process to review and ensure the currency of its published guidance.

Specifically, OFAC amended 11 FAQs (10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) to provide updated information and clarity on these critical compliance topics. These FAQs cover various aspects of sanctions compliance, including the procedures for handling blocked property and reporting requirements.

Financial institutions and other U.S. persons are advised to review these amended FAQs to ensure their internal compliance programs and reporting mechanisms align with the latest OFAC guidance. Adherence to these guidelines is essential for mitigating sanctions risks.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This action reflects a dynamic approach to sanctions implementation, balancing enforcement with humanitarian and economic considerations.

For Iran, OFAC issued General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and General License HH, authorizing wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026.

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. The agency also removed specific designations related to Belarus and North Korea, and amended several Frequently Asked Questions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Chinese Entities Under PAIPA for Intellectual Property Theft
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), targeting five entities connected to People's Republic of China national Linwei Ding for theft of trade secrets from U.S. persons.

The designated entities include Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co Ltd (Zhisuan), Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd (MiraclePlus), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Phase I), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (Phase II), and Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Zhiyuan Enterprise Management Center Limited Partnership (Zhiyuan Enterprise). These entities are alleged to have been involved in efforts to replicate Google's super intelligence (SI) infrastructure technology using stolen trade secrets.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026, with an exception for Zhisuan.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License, GL 60A, titled 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This amendment replaces and supersedes the previous GL 60.

The updated General License extends the authorization period for earthquake relief efforts from its original end date of October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027. This extension aims to facilitate ongoing humanitarian aid and recovery operations in Venezuela following recent earthquakes in the Yumare–Morón region.

In conjunction with GL 60A, OFAC also amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) 1263 to reflect the extended authorization end date, providing clarity for U.S. persons and entities involved in humanitarian efforts in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related and Cuba designations, coupled with the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions. This action underscores the U.S. government's continued pressure on both regimes.

The Iran-related designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities. For Cuba, this action follows recent significant changes to the U.S. sanctions framework, including new Cuba Sanctions Regulations (CSR) and amendments to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR).

The new and amended General Licenses and FAQs aim to provide guidance on the scope of permissible activities under the updated sanctions regimes, particularly concerning financial transactions and travel to Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action signifies a targeted adjustment to the sanctions program concerning Venezuela.

The individual removed from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) list is Jorge Rodriguez, who has served as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly since 2021 and previously as vice president under Hugo Chavez. Rodriguez was initially designated in 2018.
The delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons attempting to deal with him, reflecting a potential shift in U.S. policy towards certain Venezuelan officials.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt illicit networks that threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

These designations aim to sever financial ties and block assets of those facilitating drug trafficking and terrorist financing globally. The specific individuals and entities designated were not detailed in the initial announcement but are subject to asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

This move reinforces the U.S. commitment to combating global illicit activities and underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for financial institutions to identify and mitigate risks associated with such networks.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations, which occurred between September 18, 2021, and April 24, 2025, involved processing payments through blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for exact name and date of birth matches to blocked persons, delays in updating watchlists, and mishandling business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error. The total value of these transactions was approximately $14,834,082.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This settlement is part of a broader coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering and BSA compliance failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based logistics company and freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The apparent violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the shipment of equipment from a designated supplier in China and failed to identify the equipment as such due to deficiencies in its compliance review and program. The company also initially failed to respond fully to an OFAC administrative subpoena.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. This action highlights the significant sanctions risks faced by logistics and freight forwarding companies, particularly concerning dealings in blocked property, and underscores the importance of effective, risk-based compliance controls.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Designating Nearly 1,600 Individuals and Entities
body: The European Union has adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, a significant development that primarily focuses on extensive new listings. This package adds 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The measures were adopted in response to Russia's continuing aggression against Ukraine and recent attacks on civilian infrastructure. The centerpiece of the package is a large-scale listing exercise targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, including businesses involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

The package has been implemented through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2279 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2281. Notably, this package emphasizes additional designations and asset freezes rather than introducing new material restrictions on trade, shipping, energy, or financial activities.

articles.headline: EU Council Removes Two Businessmen from Belarus Sanctions List
body: The EU Council has updated its sanctions regime targeting Belarus, under Council Decision 2012/642/CFSP and Council Regulation (EC) 765/2006, to remove two businessmen from the sanctions list. This adjustment reflects a review of individual designations within the existing framework.

One of the delisted individuals is Mikhail Gutseriev, a prominent Russian businessman with interests in Belarus's energy, potash, and hospitality sectors. Gutseriev had been previously designated on the grounds of benefiting from and supporting the Lukashenka regime.

While removed from the Belarus sanctions list, Gutseriev remains listed under the EU's Russia asset freeze sanctions regime. The EU Council also adopted restrictive measures against 77 individuals involved in illegal Russian State Duma elections held in September 2026 in occupied territories of Ukraine.

articles.headline: EU Renews Autonomous Sanctions Against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda Until October 2027
body: The Council of the European Union has renewed its autonomous restrictive measures against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda, and associated persons, groups, undertakings, and entities. The duration of these sanctions has been prolonged for another year, until October 31, 2027.

The autonomous list currently includes 15 persons and 8 groups, all of whom are subject to an asset freeze. Additionally, individuals on the list are subject to a travel ban to the EU, and EU persons and entities are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them.

These measures complement those imposed by the UN Security Council against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda, underscoring the EU's commitment to countering the ongoing terrorist threat posed by these organizations and their regional affiliates.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends Three Entries on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On October 26, 2026, the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida, and associated individuals, groups, undertakings, and entities, enacted amendments to three entries on its ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

These amendments involve specific changes, indicated with strikethrough and underline, to the entries of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).
An updated list is accessible on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee's website, and the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List is also updated to reflect these changes.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Removes Three Entries from ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On October 24, 2026, the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida, and associated individuals, groups, undertakings, and entities, removed three entries from the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.

The entries were deleted after the Committee concluded its consideration of the delisting requests for these names, which were submitted by the designating State in accordance with paragraph 75 of resolution 2734 (2024).

The names of the individuals and entities removed from the list are available in the 'Press Releases' section of the Committee's website. This action reflects the ongoing review and adjustment of UN sanctions lists based on new information and delisting procedures.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Delists Swiss Company from Iraq Sanctions List
body: On October 5, 2026, the UN Security Council Committee decided to delist LOGARCHEO S.A., a Swiss company, from the corresponding UN sanctions list related to Iraq. This decision follows a review of the company's status.

LOGARCHEO S.A. had been subject to EU sanctions since 2006 due to its alleged association with the regime of former Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. The delisting by the UN Committee removes the basis for these restrictive measures.

As a result of this delisting, LOGARCHEO S.A. is no longer subject to the restrictive measures applicable under the EU Iraq sanctions regime, which included an asset freeze and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available.

articles.headline: U.S. Treasury Warns Foreign Financial Institutions on Iran Business Under 'Operation Economic Outcast'
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an alert to foreign financial institutions, warning them about continued business with Iran or its financial sector under 'Operation Economic Outcast.' The alert emphasizes that institutions transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could face sanctions without prior notification.

This warning follows Treasury's expansion of secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13902, targeting individuals and entities supporting Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping sectors. Recent actions include severing U.S. correspondent banking access for Banque Misr UAE and designating Türkiye-based Golden Global Bank for facilitating transactions for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force.

Foreign financial institutions facilitating Iran's access to the global financial system, including through subsidiaries or branches in third countries, risk being sanctioned for operating in or supporting sanctioned sectors of Iran's economy. OFAC urges immediate termination of such activities and relationships to avoid civil and criminal enforcement penalties.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,529,685 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty stems from apparent violations of U.S. sanctions against Russia.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and related services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard, which is blocked by operation of law due to its ownership by a designated entity.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed by Extreme Networks but were also egregious, leading to the substantial penalty. This case highlights the importance of stringent compliance measures for companies dealing with international trade, especially concerning sanctioned entities.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Civil Penalty for Sanctions Breaches
body: Bank of America, N.A. has paid a civil penalty of $11,662,930 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.

The violations included processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to properly handle alerts for sanctioned individuals, and delays in updating watchlists. These breaches occurred across sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

OFAC characterized the violations as non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This penalty was part of a coordinated enforcement action that also saw Bank of America face significant fines from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering deficiencies.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has been assessed a civil penalty of $175,015 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The penalty addresses apparent violations of OFAC's counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations stemmed from the company's arrangement of a shipment from a designated Chinese supplier without adequate sanctions screening, and an initial failure to fully respond to an OFAC administrative subpoena.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. This enforcement action serves as a reminder to logistics and freight forwarding companies about the critical need for robust compliance programs to prevent dealings with blocked persons and property.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 Related to Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has settled with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $3,777,000 concerning apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations. This substantial penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals.

The details of the individual's actions leading to the violations were not immediately disclosed in the public record, but such penalties typically involve unauthorized transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities or individuals connected to the Syrian regime.

This enforcement action serves as a strong deterrent, reminding all U.S. persons and entities of their obligations to comply with OFAC regulations and the severe consequences of engaging in prohibited activities with sanctioned jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Global Markets Show Mixed Performance Amid Inflation Concerns
body: Global financial markets are exhibiting mixed performance as investors grapple with persistent inflation concerns and varying economic indicators across major regions. While some indices show modest gains, others are experiencing downward pressure, reflecting uncertainty about future monetary policy and economic growth.

Central banks worldwide continue to monitor inflation closely, with expectations of further interest rate adjustments influencing market sentiment. Energy prices remain a key factor, contributing to inflationary pressures and impacting corporate earnings.

Analysts suggest that market volatility is likely to persist in the near term as geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions continue to affect global trade and economic stability. Investors are advised to remain cautious and diversified.

articles.headline: UN High Commissioner Condemns New US Sanctions on International Criminal Court
body: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has described the imposition of institutional sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) by the United States as 'unacceptable.' He called for immediate measures to protect the Court and individuals cooperating with it.

The U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly vowed to 'dismantle the ICC, brick by brick' unless it ends what Washington considers a 'threat' to its citizens. These sanctions are the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel.

Türk urged the 125 States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court to take urgent steps to defend the Court's crucial work and ensure its ability to function, emphasizing their obligation to protect the institution they created.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against American Express and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, detailing various penalties against financial institutions and institution-affiliated parties. These actions are taken to ensure timely correction of deficient practices and violations.

Notable actions include a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and identification program violations.

Additionally, Bank of America, National Association, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals for embezzlement.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
